cards.front: A {{c1::motor unit}} is one alpha motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it innervates.
cards.back: A motor pool, by contrast, is all the motor neurons that supply one muscle.
cards.quote: A motor unit is one alpha motor neuron and all the fibres it innervates
cards.section: Motor units: where every command ends

cards.front: In the spinal cord, where do the cell bodies of alpha motor neurons sit, and by which route do their axons leave the cord?
cards.back: Cell bodies in the ventral horn; axons leave through the ventral roots.
cards.quote: alpha motor neurons, whose cell bodies sit in the ventral horn of the cord and whose axons leave through the ventral roots
cards.section: Motor units: where every command ends

cards.front: Why is a motor unit the smallest piece of force the spinal cord can command?
cards.back: Normally each motor-neuron spike gives every fibre of the unit an action potential and a twitch, so the unit contracts as a whole.
cards.why: In mature muscle each fibre is contacted by one motor neuron, so a fibre cannot be driven apart from its unit.
cards.quote: normally each motor-neuron spike gives every fibre of its unit an action potential and a twitch
cards.section: Motor units: where every command ends

cards.front: What did Sherrington call alpha motor neurons, and why?
cards.back: The final common path: every command that makes a limb muscle contract has to pass through them.
cards.quote: Every command that makes a limb muscle contract has to pass through these motor neurons.
cards.section: Motor units: where every command ends

cards.front: A cell's {{c1::input resistance}}, R_in, is how many millivolts its voltage changes for each nanoampere of steady current put into it.
cards.back: Bathtub picture: fewer drains, so the same inflow raises the water level higher.
cards.quote: A cell's input resistance, R_in, is how many millivolts its voltage changes for each nanoampere of steady current put into it.
cards.section: Motor units: where every command ends

cards.front: In the guiding rule for spinal motor control, how does any command reach a muscle, and when does a motor neuron fire?
cards.back: Every command arrives as synaptic current onto motor neurons; excitation adds current and inhibition, in effect, takes it away. A motor neuron fires when net current times its input resistance lifts it to threshold.
cards.quote: A motor neuron fires when the net current, times its input resistance, lifts it to threshold
cards.section: Motor units: where every command ends

cards.front: Under a shared, slowly rising input, motor neurons in a pool are recruited small before large: the {{c1::size principle}}.
cards.back: A tendency under shared input, first measured in cats, not a law.
cards.quote: This order, small before large, is the size principle.
cards.section: The size principle: small before large

cards.front: Why does a small motor neuron have a higher input resistance than a large one?
cards.back: Current must leave through open membrane channels. A small cell has less membrane, so fewer channels in parallel: fewer drains, higher resistance.
cards.quote: A small cell has less membrane, so fewer channels in parallel and a higher input resistance: fewer drains.
cards.section: The size principle: small before large

cards.front: Using Ohm's law, write the current a motor neuron needs to reach threshold, and say what it implies for recruitment order.
cards.back: I_th = ΔV_th / R_in. With equal required depolarizations and the same slowly rising effective current, the higher-resistance cell reaches threshold earlier; more generally, small cells go first when effective current grows less steeply with size than resistance falls.
cards.why: Unit force does not directly set the electrical threshold: firing depends on how far the input moves the voltage.
cards.quote: Higher input resistance means less current is needed, so the cell is recruited earlier.
cards.section: The size principle: small before large

cards.front: A large motor neuron has room for more synapses. Under what condition do small cells in a pool still reach threshold first?
cards.back: With equal required depolarizations, whenever effective current grows less steeply with cell size than input resistance falls. If current grew as steeply, the two would cancel.
cards.why: For spindle input in cat medial gastrocnemius motor neurons, effective current was on average larger, not smaller, in high-resistance cells, reinforcing their head start.
cards.quote: the small cells still go first whenever effective current grows less steeply with size than input resistance falls
cards.section: The size principle: small before large

cards.front: Why is recruiting the small motor units of a pool first useful for movement?
cards.back: Small units make small forces, so the first steps of force are tiny, which is when an error of a fraction of a newton matters most, as in threading a needle.
cards.quote: Recruiting them first makes the first steps of force tiny, which is when an error of a fraction of a newton matters most
cards.section: The size principle: small before large

cards.front: An input reaches only the large motor neurons of a pool, not the small ones. As that input rises, which units are recruited first, and does the size principle hold?
cards.back: Large units can be recruited first, out of size order. The size principle is a tendency under shared input, so an input confined to part of the pool can break it.
cards.why: Threshold differences, persistent inward currents and neuromodulation can also shift the order.
cards.quote: an input that reaches only part of a pool can recruit cells out of size order
cards.section: The size principle: small before large

cards.front: Three motor neurons in one pool get the same synaptic current, ramped from 0 at 2 nA per second. Input resistances: A 5.0 MΩ, B 2.5 MΩ, C 0.5 MΩ. Each must depolarize 10 mV to fire (steady state). Give each cell's threshold current and firing time, and the order.
cards.back: I_th = 10 mV / R_in (mV/MΩ = nA): A 2 nA, B 4 nA, C 20 nA. At 2 nA/s: A at 1 s, B at 2 s, C at 10 s. Highest input resistance first: A, then B, then C.
cards.quote: A millivolt divided by a megohm is a nanoampere.

cards.front: Motor units with forces of 0.1 N, 0.4 N and 2.0 N are recruited in that order. Give the total force after each recruit, and describe how the size of each step changes.
cards.back: 0.1 N, then 0.5 N, then 2.5 N. The steps get bigger as force grows, because later recruits are stronger units.
cards.quote: As each joins, total force goes 0.05 N, then 0.35 N, then 1.85 N.

cards.front: Name the two ways the spinal cord raises a muscle's force.
cards.back: Recruitment (adding motor units) and rate coding (driving the active units to fire faster).
cards.quote: So force rises both by adding units and by driving the active ones harder.

cards.front: Why does firing a motor unit faster raise its force?
cards.back: Each new twitch starts before the last has relaxed, so it rides on top of it and force climbs; closer still, the ripples merge into a fused plateau, a tetanus.
cards.quote: each new twitch starts before the last has relaxed, so it rides on top of it and the line climbs higher

cards.front: When spikes come so close that a unit's twitch ripples merge into a smooth, high plateau, the fused contraction is called a {{c1::tetanus}}.
cards.back: Fusion means smooth force, not necessarily the unit's maximum force.
cards.quote: the ripples merge into a smooth, high plateau, a tetanus

cards.front: During ordinary voluntary contractions most motor units fire below fusion. Why is the muscle's force still smooth?
cards.back: Its many units fire out of step with each other, so their force ripples fill one another's gaps.
cards.quote: The muscle's force is smooth largely because its many units fire out of step with each other, so their ripples fill one another's gaps.

cards.front: A slow motor unit (long twitch) and a fast unit (short twitch) both fire at 20 Hz. Which gives the smoother force, and why?
cards.back: The slow unit. Its long twitches overlap more at the same rate, so slow units tend to fuse at lower firing rates than fast ones.
cards.why: In one illustrative linear model, ripple at 20 Hz was about 4.7% for a slow twitch and 28% for a fast one.
cards.quote: slow units tend to fuse at lower firing rates than fast ones

cards.front: In human vastus lateralis, units past their initial steep rise increased firing by a mean of 2.0 pulses per second per 10% of maximal force. A tracked unit fires at 8 pulses per second at 20% of maximal force and follows the mean. Predict its rate at 50%.
cards.back: 50% − 20% = three 10% steps: 8 + 3 × 2.0 = 14 pulses per second. The rise in an already-recruited unit is rate coding.
cards.quote: firing rates rose between force plateaus 10% of maximal force apart by 3.5 ± 1.7 pulses per second in tibialis anterior and 2.0 ± 1.1 in vastus lateralis

cards.front: Why does a muscle spindle report the muscle's length?
cards.back: Its intrafusal fibres lie parallel to the force-making extrafusal fibres, like a thread laid along a rope, so when the muscle lengthens, the spindle lengthens with it.
cards.quote: When the muscle lengthens, the spindle lengthens with it, so it reports length.

cards.front: In relaxed human muscle, what do spindle Ia afferents and group II afferents each respond to?
cards.back: Ia (primary): both the speed and the amount of stretch. Group II (secondary): mainly the amount.
cards.quote: In relaxed human muscle, Ia afferents respond to both the speed and the amount of stretch

cards.front: Trace the excitatory arm of the stretch reflex after a tendon tap.
cards.back: Stretch fires spindle Ia afferents, which enter through the dorsal root and excite the homonymous motor neurons directly (one synapse, monosynaptic). The muscle contracts against the stretch.
cards.why: This helps hold a joint: a sudden stretch from an unexpected load is met by contraction of the stretched muscle.
cards.quote: One branch excites the motor neurons of the same muscle, the homonymous motor neurons, directly: one synapse, a monosynaptic path.

cards.front: A Ia afferent releases only an excitatory transmitter. How does a quadriceps stretch inhibit the hamstring motor neurons on the same side?
cards.back: A Ia branch excites a Ia inhibitory interneuron on the same side, which inhibits the antagonist's motor neurons: a disynaptic, ipsilateral path. The interneuron changes the sign.
cards.quote: In this fast pathway the Ia afferent itself makes only excitatory synapses; the inhibitory interneuron changes the sign.

cards.front: Inhibition of the antagonist's motor neurons when a muscle is stretched is the inhibitory half of reciprocal innervation, called {{c1::reciprocal inhibition}}.
cards.quote: Sherrington called this pairing of excitation and inhibition reciprocal innervation; its inhibitory half is called reciprocal inhibition.

cards.front: Ia inhibitory interneurons on the left side of the lumbar cord are destroyed. The left patellar tendon is tapped. Predict the effect on left quadriceps and left hamstring motor neurons.
cards.back: The direct excitation of left quadriceps motor neurons remains, so the kick's excitatory arm is preserved. The described fast, disynaptic Ia inhibition of left hamstring motor neurons is lost.
cards.why: The excitatory path is monosynaptic and needs no interneuron; this fast inhibitory pathway to the antagonist runs through the Ia inhibitory interneuron.
cards.quote: Another branch excites a Ia inhibitory interneuron on the same side of the cord, which inhibits the motor neurons of the antagonist

cards.front: In an animal, the ventral roots serving one leg are cut and the dorsal roots are left intact. The patellar tendon is tapped. Do the spindle Ia afferents fire, and does the quadriceps contract?
cards.back: The Ia afferents fire and their signal enters the cord, but the quadriceps does not contract.
cards.why: Sensory axons enter through the dorsal root; motor axons leave through the ventral roots, so the efferent limb is cut.
cards.quote: They enter the cord through the dorsal root and branch.

cards.front: Where is the Golgi tendon organ, and what does it signal that the spindle does not?
cards.back: At the muscle-tendon junction, in series with a small group of muscle fibres. It senses the tension they pass to the tendon, so tendon organs signal force rather than length.
cards.quote: It senses the tension those fibres pass to the tendon, and together the tendon organs signal the force the muscle makes rather than its length.
cards.section: The tendon organ: a force sensor

cards.front: One motor unit twitches, its fibres pulling on a single tendon organ, and the muscle is free to shorten a little. Predict the firing of that tendon organ and of a nearby spindle.
cards.back: The tendon organ fires; the spindle's firing drops or stops.
cards.why: The tendon organ is in series and feels the pull. The spindle lies parallel to fibres that just shortened, so it shortens too and can fall slack.
cards.quote: The spindle lies alongside fibres that have just shortened, so it shortens too and can fall slack
cards.section: The tendon organ: a force sensor

cards.front: What does the textbook Ib (tendon organ) pathway do to the muscle's own motor pool, and is it simply a safety cutout?
cards.back: Acting through interneurons, it inhibits the muscle's own motor neurons. It is not simply a safety cutout against tearing: real Ib effects change with the task.
cards.quote: The textbook pathway pushes the muscle's own pool down, inhibiting its motor neurons.
cards.section: The tendon organ: a force sensor

cards.front: A person steps on a tack with the right foot. Predict which of the four groups of leg muscles (right and left flexors and extensors) are pushed up and which down.
cards.back: Right flexors up (the leg withdraws), right extensors down; left flexors down, left extensors up (the leg takes the weight).
cards.why: Crossed-extensor reflex: polysynaptic and bilateral, with interneuron axons crossing the midline; reciprocal innervation across both legs.
cards.quote: In the classic pattern two groups go up and two go down: reciprocal innervation again, now across both legs.
cards.section: The crossed-extensor reflex: four groups of pools at once

cards.front: What do gamma motor neurons innervate?
cards.back: Muscle spindles only: the contractile poles of the intrafusal fibres.
cards.quote: They supply muscle spindles only, ending on the contractile poles of the intrafusal fibres.
cards.section: Gamma: keeping the spindle in range

cards.front: What does alpha-gamma coactivation achieve during a contraction?
cards.back: Gamma drive contracts the spindle's poles, pulling its centre taut. During alpha-gamma coactivation, this can keep the spindle from falling slack as the muscle shortens, so the stretch circuit can retain its length signal.
cards.quote: the spindle can be kept from falling slack during a contraction, so the stretch circuit keeps its length signal just as the muscle moves
cards.section: Gamma: keeping the spindle in range

cards.front: Gamma motor neurons to the biceps are silenced while alpha drive is intact. The biceps shortens voluntarily. Predict its spindle Ia firing during the shortening.
cards.back: Without gamma tightening, shortening can leave the spindle slack, so Ia firing may drop or stop and the length signal may be reduced or lost.
cards.why: Gamma drive is what normally tightens the spindle's centre as the muscle shortens.
cards.quote: The twitch in the last check exposed a problem: a shortening muscle can leave its spindle slack and silent.
cards.section: Gamma: keeping the spindle in range

cards.front: Microneurography of single Ia afferents from human wrist and finger extensors during an instructed delay showed Ia firing fell after a cue when the coming reach would stretch the muscle, with no systematic change in kinematics or surface EMG. What can be concluded about gamma drive, and what limits the conclusion?
cards.back: The results suggest that gamma drive may be tuned to the coming movement rather than simply tracking alpha drive. This is an indirect interpretation compatible with the Ia recordings; gamma neurons were not recorded, and the main analysis used eight afferents from six people.
cards.quote: Ia firing fell when the coming reach would stretch the spindle-bearing muscle, while kinematics and surface EMG showed no systematic change with the target.
cards.section: A spindle that changes before you move

cards.front: Graham Brown cut the spinal cord of cats and also cut the dorsal roots from the hind limbs. What did the view that walking is a chain of reflexes predict, what was seen, and what does it show?
cards.back: The chain view predicted no rhythm. Instead the ankle flexors and extensors still contracted in alternation, so the rhythm arises within the cord.
cards.quote: Instead, the ankle flexors and extensors still contracted in alternation.

cards.front: A {{c1::central pattern generator}} is a neural network capable of producing rhythmic output without patterned descending or sensory input.
cards.back: Often studied as fictive locomotion: locomotor-like motor output with no movement.
cards.quote: A central pattern generator is a neural network capable of producing rhythmic output without patterned descending or sensory input.

cards.front: Describe Graham Brown's half-centre model of the locomotor rhythm and how activity switches.
cards.back: Two groups of neurons, one driving flexors and one driving extensors, inhibit each other. Activity switches when the active group's inhibition fades, or when the held-down group recovers and escapes.
cards.why: Whether the rhythm comes from a simple pair of half-centres is still debated.
cards.quote: two groups of neurons, one driving flexors and one driving extensors, that inhibit each other

cards.front: The stretch reflex and the half-centre model of locomotion share one circuit motif. Name it and contrast how each uses it.
cards.back: Reciprocal inhibition. In the stretch reflex it pairs excitation of one pool with inhibition of the antagonist pool at the same moment; in the half-centre, mutual inhibition alternates flexor and extensor drive over time.
cards.quote: It is reciprocal inhibition laid out in time.

cards.front: During a step, a spinal rhythm generator pushes the extensor pool of one leg up with slowly rising drive. Within that pool, which motor units join first, and how does force keep rising once all units you are watching are active?
cards.back: Under shared drive satisfying the size-principle conditions, small, weak units tend to join before larger ones. Force can then rise through rate coding as active units fire faster and their twitches sum, while their firing and force responses have not saturated.
cards.why: The rhythm reaches muscle as synaptic current onto motor neurons, like every other command, so the within-pool rules still apply.
cards.quote: Within each pool, the second question still applies.

cards.front: Before stimulating an ankle nerve to test resetting of the locomotor rhythm in an isolated neonatal mouse cord, why are the ventral roots transected proximal to the spinal nerve?
cards.back: So the stimulus pulses cannot travel back into the cord along motor axons; any reset must come from sensory input.
cards.quote: so pulses cannot travel back into the cord along motor axons

cards.front: An isolated neonatal mouse spinal cord bathed in NMDA and serotonin shows alternating flexor-related and extensor-related ventral-root bursts. Which two controls show that this pattern is evoked by the drugs?
cards.back: Record baseline activity in saline before adding the drugs, since neonatal cords can burst on their own, and check that the locomotor pattern fades on washout.
cards.quote: record baseline activity in saline before adding the drugs, since neonatal cords can burst on their own

cards.front: A drug-driven isolated neonatal rodent cord produces a locomotor rhythm with no patterned input. What does this result fail to show?
cards.back: It does not show adult or human walking, does not identify a single pacemaker cell, and does not prove that normal walking dispenses with the brain or feedback. It shows the circuit is enough under these conditions.
cards.why: For people, evidence for a spinal pattern generator is indirect.
cards.quote: it does not identify a single pacemaker cell or prove that normal walking dispenses with the brain or with feedback

cards.front: Optogenetic activation in the isolated neonatal mouse cord induced locomotor-like bursting on one side alone. What does this show?
cards.back: Rhythmic bursting does not need the other side of the cord.
cards.quote: locomotor-like bursting could be induced on one side alone, so rhythmic bursting does not need the other side of the cord

cards.front: A reflex path runs 0.40 m from muscle to cord and 0.40 m back, at a conduction velocity of 64 m/s. What is the conduction time, and what fraction of it would one extra central synapse of 0.5 to 1 ms add?
cards.back: 0.80 m / 64 m/s = 12.5 ms. An extra 0.5 to 1 ms is 4 to 8% of that.
cards.why: Time = distance / velocity. A single central synapse keeps the delay inside the cord to a minimum.
cards.quote: the path between knee and cord is about 0.55 m each way, so at 60 to 70 m/s conduction alone takes about 16 to 18 ms

cards.front: Assume all cells require the same depolarization to reach threshold and receive a slowly rising shared drive. Suppose a motor neuron's effective input grows with membrane area A as A^1, and its input resistance falls as A^−0.8. For cells of relative area 1, 2 and 4, give the relative depolarizations and the recruitment order.
cards.back: ΔV ∝ A^(α−β) = A^0.2: 1, 1.15, 1.32. The large cell depolarizes most, so recruitment would run large before small, reversing the size principle.
cards.why: Rests on the scaling rule: small first only when current grows less steeply with size than resistance falls (α < β). Hypothetical case, not a measured law.
cards.quote: Then the depolarization scales as ΔV ∝ A^(α−β).
cards.section: How the input scales with cell size

cards.front: In a passive model, a cell rests at −70 mV, fires at −60 mV, has input resistance 2 MΩ, and has an inhibitory reversal potential of −80 mV. How much steady excitatory current does it need to reach threshold with an inhibitory conductance of 0.15 µS?
cards.back: Leak: 10 mV / 2 MΩ = 5.0 nA. Inhibitory current at threshold: 0.15 µS × (−60 − (−80)) mV = 3.0 nA. Total 8.0 nA, versus 5.0 nA with no inhibition.
cards.why: Inhibition opens channels, so the excitatory current must cover both the leak and the inhibitory current at threshold.
cards.quote: Inhibition does not literally subtract current; it opens channels.
